15.title: the women went to the tomb first
15.hook: the women went to the tomb first
15.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter as their greatest feast, often with a vigil the night before or a service at sunrise. Many greet each other with "Christ is risen" and answer "he is risen indeed." Orthodox churches often keep Easter on a later date, by an older calendar.

screen: `DAY FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cross. Rome's execution, and now the most recognized sign on earth. Your line: the worst thing is not the last thing. Did you need it? Day fifteen.

It's very early on a Sunday, first light. Three women are walking to a grave, carrying spices. Their friend was executed on Friday, and there wasn't time to prepare his body before the Sabbath, so they're going now. It's the last thing you can do for someone you love: take care of them after they're gone. And on the way, they realize they have a problem. The tomb is sealed with a stone, a big one, and none of them can move it. Mark's Gospel keeps the question they ask each other on the road: "Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?" Today's word starts with that question.
screen: `SUNDAY. FIRST LIGHT.` → `THREE WOMEN, CARRYING SPICES.` → `WHO WILL MOVE THE STONE?`

segments.voice: Easter. In most of the world its name comes from Pascha, from the Hebrew word for Passover, because it happened in Passover week. Where the English word Easter comes from, nobody is completely sure. Here's how Mark tells it. The women arrive, and the stone is already rolled back. Inside sits a young man dressed in white, who tells them: "he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." And the oldest copies of Mark end almost right there. The women run from the tomb, trembling, and say nothing to anyone, "for they were afraid." Fear, and an empty room. The longer endings in many Bibles were added later; most scholars agree on that, and many churches still read them. John tells it closer up. Mary Magdalene comes alone, while it's still dark, and finds the stone gone. She stays outside, crying. A man asks why she's weeping, and she thinks he's the gardener. Then he says one word. Her name. "Mary." And she knows him. Now notice who's there first. Not Peter. Not the twelve. Women, in a world where a woman's word counted for little. Every Gospel puts them at the tomb first. Many historians say that's not a detail anyone would make up to impress people. Easter is the center of the Christian year. Christians say Jesus rose from the dead, and that death doesn't get the last word. On Easter morning many greet each other: Christ is risen. And the answer comes back: he is risen indeed. The women's question on the road was how to move the stone. By the time they got there, it was already moved.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and it's a little longer now: seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe. Think of a stone in your life right now. Something heavy in the way, that you've been worrying about on the road, before you've even gotten there. Name it. Now, just for this minute, picture walking up and finding it already moved. Don't plan how. Don't argue with it. Just let yourself feel the relief, and breathe into it. If you pray, you can hand the stone over. If you don't, just notice how much of the weight was the worrying. The bell holds the time.
Easter. Pascha. The morning the stone was moved and the tomb was empty. Fifteenth word.

16.title: David shouting at God
16.hook: David shouting at God — anger is allowed
16.carry: you can say anything to him
16.howItsDone: Christians sing and pray the Psalms in church services and at home. In monasteries, and in the daily prayer of some churches, the Psalms are prayed in order over a set cycle.

screen: `DAY SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter. The women at the tomb at first light. Your line: the stone is already moved. Did you catch yourself worrying on the road? Day sixteen.

Anger at a person. Anger at a life. Sometimes, anger at God, or the universe, or whoever runs things. It can seem like the one feeling nobody brings to church, where everyone shows up polite. Now open the middle of the Bible, and there's a whole book of people who didn't. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" That's not a complaint about God. It's a complaint to God, out loud, and it's scripture. Today's word is that book.
screen: `ANGER, EVEN AT GOD.` → `CHURCH CLOTHES, POLITE FACES.` → `"HOW LONG?"`

segments.voice: The Psalms. A hundred and fifty poems, the songbook of ancient Israel, still prayed by Jews and by Christians. The name comes from Greek, psalmos, a song sung to a plucked string instrument. The Hebrew title is Tehillim: praises. Tradition ties many of them to David, the shepherd boy who became king. The headings put his name on about half of them; scholars debate how many he actually wrote. For a book called praises, a great deal of it is complaint. Scholars call these laments, and there are a lot of them. Psalm 13 opens: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" It asks how long four times. Psalm 22 begins with the line from the cross you heard two days ago: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" And Psalm 88 ends in darkness, with no comfort at all. It just stops. These weren't hidden away. Many carry headings addressed to the chief musician: songs to be sung. Laments often have a shape. First the honest part: where are you, this isn't fair, I'm going under. Then, often, a turn. Psalm 13, after all its how longs, ends by saying the singer has trusted in God's mercy and will sing again. In these songs, the anger doesn't have to be cleaned up first. It's the way in. Monks, soldiers, prisoners and people in hospital beds have prayed the Psalms down the centuries. There's room in them for grief, fear and fury, as well as praise.

Then just breathe, and notice what's left once it's been said. You don't have to fix anything. The bell holds the time.

17.title: not certainty
17.tomorrow: Elijah: not the wind, not the earthquake
17.howItsDone: Christians describe faith as trust in God, and in times of doubt some pray the father's line from Mark: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

screen: `DAY SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Psalms. A hundred and fifty songs, and plenty of them shouting. Your line: you can say anything to him. Did you say one true thing? Day seventeen.

Some people seem to have faith like a wall. Solid, certain, never shaken. Next to that, anyone with questions, bad weeks, or mornings of not being sure of anything can start to think faith belongs to other people. Here's a scene from Mark's Gospel. A father brings his son to Jesus. The boy has suffered since childhood, and the disciples couldn't help. The father says: if you can do anything, help us. Jesus tells him all things are possible to the one who believes. And the father cries out, in tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. Today's word.
screen: `FAITH LIKE A WALL?` → `A FATHER, OUT OF OPTIONS.` → `"I BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF."`

segments.voice: Faith. The Greek word is pistis, and it's less about certainty than about trust. It's the word for trusting a friend, or being faithful to one. It can mean loyalty. You have faith in someone the way you have faith in a bridge: not because you've proved it, but because you're willing to put your weight on it. Remember day one? Amen, from the Hebrew root for firm, solid. Same idea. Now, how much of it do you need? Matthew tells the same story as Mark. Afterward, the disciples ask Jesus why they couldn't help the boy themselves. And he says: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." A mustard seed. A tiny thing. He doesn't say: if you had enormous faith. He says: if you had even this much. The mountain is big. The seed is tiny. The point is the seed. Back on day five the mustard seed was a picture of the kingdom; here it's the size of faith. The letter to the Hebrews has another line: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." Not seen. In that line, faith is what you have exactly when you can't see. So some Christian writers have said that doubt isn't simply faith's opposite, and can even be where faith lives. The father in Mark didn't bring a perfect faith. He brought a half-sure, crying, both-at-once faith, and the story doesn't send him away. Jesus heals the boy. Some Christians read that as: enough to start with. In this story, faith looks less like a feeling of certainty and more like one small step of trust, taken while still not sure.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. If there's something tiny nearby, a grain of rice, a seed, a crumb, put it in your palm. If not, just open your hand. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're unsure about. Don't solve it. Just admit it. Now think of one small thing you do trust. The floor holding you up. The next breath coming. One person. Let that small thing be enough, for now. If you pray, the father's words are there for you: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. The bell holds the time.
Faith. Pistis. Not certainty: trust, even the size of a seed. Seventeenth word.

18.title: Elijah: not the wind, not the earthquake
18.hook: Elijah: not the wind, not the earthquake — the still small voice
18.tomorrow: a table, bread, wine, remember me
18.howItsDone: Christians keep times of silent prayer, alone or together. Monasteries keep hours of silence, Quaker meetings wait in silence together, and some retreats ask people to keep quiet for days.

screen: `DAY EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith. Pistis: trust, even the size of a mustard seed. Your line: small is enough. What small step did you take? Day eighteen.

A showdown on a mountain. Fire from heaven. A whole crowd face down on the ground. That was one prophet's day. Then one threat from a queen, and he runs. He goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits down under a juniper tree, and says: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life." Anyone who has crashed right after a high may recognize him. His name is Elijah, a prophet of Israel. And what happens next is very quiet.
screen: `FIRE ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `ONE THREAT, AND HE RUNS.` → `"IT IS ENOUGH."`

segments.voice: Silence. First, notice what happens before anything spiritual. An angel wakes Elijah and tells him: arise and eat. There's bread baked on hot stones, and a jar of water. He eats, sleeps, and eats again. Food and rest, before a single word of teaching. Then he walks for forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God, and hides in a cave. He's told to go and stand on the mountain, because the Lord is about to pass by. Here it is, in the King James: "a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice." Wind, earthquake, fire. The places you'd expect God to show up. And not there. Then, a still small voice. The Hebrew is stranger than the English. Kol demamah dakah. Kol is a voice, or a sound. Demamah is stillness, silence. Dakah is thin, or fine. A sound of thin silence. Translators render it in many ways, because it's almost a contradiction: a sound made of quiet. And when Elijah hears it, he wraps his face in his cloak and steps out to meet it. Christians have often read this story as a picture of prayer, and the Carmelite friars and nuns look to Elijah as a model for the life of quiet listening. The noise and the drama may come, but in this story God isn't in them. He's in the quiet right after.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Turn something off. The music, the TV, the notifications. Sit, and breathe. Notice the sounds that are left: a fridge, traffic, your own breath. Don't chase them away. Let them be the wind and the earthquake. Now listen underneath them, for the quiet itself. If you pray, you can simply listen, the way Elijah did at the mouth of the cave. If you don't, just rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Silence. Kol demamah dakah: a sound of thin silence. Eighteenth word.

19.title: a table, bread, wine, remember me
19.hook: a table, bread, wine, remember me
19.howItsDone: Christians share communion with bread and wine (or grape juice), as Jesus did at the last supper. Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at every Mass or Divine Liturgy; Protestant churches share it weekly, monthly or a few times a year; and a few groups, such as Quakers, keep no outward meal.

screen: `DAY NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence. Not the wind, not the earthquake, not the fire. A still small voice. Your line: quiet is where he is. Did you find your one quiet minute? Day nineteen.

The last dinner before someone moved away. A holiday table the week after a funeral. Years later, the menu is gone. What stays is who was there, and what somebody said. An upstairs room in Jerusalem, at Passover. Jesus and the twelve, at one table. He has just told them that one of them will betray him. And instead of a speech, he picks up the bread. That's the last supper. What he did with the bread and the cup, churches still do, in cathedrals and in kitchens, with the same few words. Today's word is that meal.
screen: `WHO WAS THERE. WHAT WAS SAID.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM. PASSOVER.` → `HE PICKS UP THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Communion. Here's a surprise first: the words Christians repeat at that table aren't only in the Gospels. They're in a letter too, and the letter may be older than any Gospel. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, passes on what he says he had received and already handed on to them. In the old King James Bible: "the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." Then the cup, and the same words again: in remembrance of me. The Greek word for remembrance is anamnesis. Christians often hear more in it than a memory in your head: a remembering you do, with your hands, so the thing is present again. Families do this at every holiday table. Jews do it at Passover, telling the story as if they'd been there. That was the meal Jesus was eating. The meal has several names. Communion, from a word Paul uses for sharing: all of us, one loaf. The Eucharist, from the Greek for giving thanks, because that's what he did first. The Lord's Supper. The Mass. And here's where Christians honestly differ, so here's who says what. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present in the bread and the wine. Not a symbol. Him. Some Protestant churches understand the meal as a memorial: the bread and wine are signs, and the remembering is the heart of it. Lutherans, Anglicans and Reformed churches each have their own careful words for how Christ is present in the meal. Churches have argued about this for centuries, and they still do. What they share is the shape of it: a table, bread, a cup, and the words, remember me.

Communion. Sharing one loaf and one cup. A meal that is a memory. Nineteenth word.

20.title: not a building
20.hook: not a building — the people; the Greek word means "the called-out ones"
20.tomorrow: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
20.howItsDone: Most Christians gather with a church on Sundays for worship, and many also meet in small groups at home during the week. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches are organized differently, but all speak of the church as the people, not the building.

screen: `DAY TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, communion. A table, bread, a cup, and the words: remember me. Your line: a meal is a memory. Did you eat one meal slowly? Day twenty.

Say the word church and a picture comes up. A steeple. Stained glass. Maybe a cathedral so big your voice echoes, maybe a strip-mall storefront with folding chairs. Everybody pictures a building. But here's a fact that surprises people. For about the first two hundred years, Christians had almost no church buildings at all. They met in kitchens and courtyards. In somebody's living room, around somebody's table. Paul ends one of his letters sending greetings to a married couple, and in the old King James he adds: "greet the church that is in their house." The church was in the house. Which means it wasn't the house. Today's word is what it was.
screen: `SAY "CHURCH." WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `200 YEARS, ALMOST NO BUILDINGS.` → `"THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE."`

segments.voice: The church. The word in the New Testament is Greek: ekklesia. It's made of two small pieces. Ek, out. And a word for calling. The called-out ones. In a Greek city, the ekklesia was the assembly: the citizens called out of their homes to gather and decide things together. It wasn't a place. It was people, showing up. So when the first Christians needed a word for themselves, that's the one they picked. Not the temple. Not a sacred site. The gathering. Paul pushes it further. He tells one of his churches: "ye are the body of Christ." Hands, feet, eyes, ears. All different. None of them the whole thing, and none of them able to say to the others, I don't need you. That's how he pictures a church: not a crowd of the same person, but a body of very different ones. And then there's the promise Jesus makes in Matthew's Gospel, the smallest possible church. "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Not two or three hundred. Christians today gather in every size and shape there is. Some in cathedrals that took centuries to build. Some in house churches, still meeting around a kitchen table the old way. Some in a hospital room, or a prison, or on a video call. Churches differ a lot about how they're led and how they're joined. But almost every one of them would say this much: the building is where the church meets. The people are the church.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Now think of the two or three people you'd call if something went wrong tonight. The ones who'd show up. Picture them, one at a time. Where they live. Their faces. And then widen it a little: someone who showed up for you once and never knew what it meant. If you pray, you can gather them in your prayer, the way Christians gather in his name. If you don't, just let them be gathered here with you for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The church. Ekklesia. Not a building: the called-out ones, gathered. Twentieth word.

what a scholar hears: ekklesia was the Greek city's assembly of citizens. early churches met in homes; one house church found at Dura-Europos in Syria dates from the third century.

21.title: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
21.hook: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead; "the beginning of the good news"
21.howItsDone: Christians hear the Gospels read aloud in church, and some churches follow a cycle of readings in which one year draws largely on Mark. Some groups read the whole of Mark aloud in one sitting.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Twenty-one days. Say them with me, fast: amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Sabbath, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes, love, the cross, Easter, the Psalms, faith, silence, communion, the church. Three weeks ago most of those were just words. Last day of Camp 1. Day twenty-one.
screen: the full strand, twenty words lit.

segments.voice: The words you just said keep circling back to four short books: the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. And the shortest of the four is Mark. Sixteen chapters. You could read the whole thing aloud in one sitting, start to finish, in somebody's living room. Some scholars think it's the oldest Gospel too. It's fast. It's blunt. It skips the parts you'd expect. There's no Christmas in it, no shepherds, no star. It starts with a man shouting in the desert. And its very first line is today's word.
screen: `FOUR SHORT BOOKS.` → `MARK: THE SHORTEST.` → `NO CHRISTMAS. A DESERT.` → `THE FIRST LINE.`

segments.voice: Mark, chapter one, verse one. In the old King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole verse. It's a title, and a door. Start with gospel: good news. Mark's Greek word is euangelion, and it wasn't a church word yet. Historians point to Roman-era inscriptions that use it for public announcements. A victory won. News about an emperor. News that changes the day for everyone who hears it. Mark takes that word and puts it on a carpenter from Galilee. Now, the shape, so you know the mountain ahead. First, Galilee: a man called by a river, fishermen dropping their nets, healings, arguments, and the stories he told. A word Mark uses again and again here is straightway. Immediately. Everything happens fast. Then, right in the middle, the turning point. Jesus asks his friends, who do you say that I am? And from there the road turns toward Jerusalem. The last third of the book is one week: the entry into the city, the table and the bread, the cross, and the empty tomb, where the women run away, afraid. Which brings us back to the first word of the book. Beginning. Some readers notice that Mark calls all of it, the whole book, just the beginning. As if the good news isn't finished when the book ends. As if the reader is supposed to pick it up from there. That's what the next camp does. Camp 2 is the stories: the ones he told, and the ones told about him. Start here.
screen: `EUANGELION — GOOD NEWS.` · `GALILEE: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE TURN: WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?` · `ONE LAST WEEK.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Last sit of the camp. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe, the way you did on day one. Remember the first word: amen. Let it be so. Now let one word from these three weeks come back to you on its own. Don't pick it. Let it arrive. Grace, maybe. Or the stone already moved. Or quiet. Hold it for a few breaths. Then ask yourself, gently: where does this start for me? If you pray, you can offer that word back as your prayer, with an amen. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be the beginning. The bell holds the time.
Mark 1:1. The beginning of the gospel. Good news, and only the beginning of it. Twenty-first word. And the strand is complete.
screen: `MARK 1:1 — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP 1. FIRST WORDS. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: start here. Tomorrow, Camp 2 begins: the stories. And it opens with a question: why did he tell stories at all? Twenty-one days. That's a practice. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY HE TOLD STORIES.`
